cards.heading: Definition
cards.question: What is "evaluation rubric as training signal"?
cards.answer: Reusing a benchmark's own grading rubric as the supervision for improving a model against it, rather than training a separate reward model or running a human relabelling pass.

cards.heading: Supervised form
cards.question: How does the rejection-sampling supervised form work?
cards.answer: Generate completions with the base model, keep only the ones that pass every rubric criterion, and fine-tune on those survivors.

cards.heading: Reinforcement form
cards.question: How does the reinforcement fine-tuning form differ from the supervised form?
cards.answer: It calls the rubric's evaluators during training so each criterion contributes its own reward, instead of filtering pre-generated completions.

cards.heading: Ceiling of rejection sampling
cards.question: Why can't rejection-sampling supervised fine-tuning teach criteria the base model never satisfies?
cards.answer: Because there are no passing samples of those criteria to imitate — the method can only reinforce behavior the model already sometimes produces.

cards.heading: Reading the reported result
cards.question: In the reported run, why did the strict all-criteria-pass count (11 to 15 of 100) matter more than the mean pass rate (0.863 to 0.876)?
cards.answer: A small mean lift with a large strict-metric jump signals a model that learned to close tasks out cleanly, not one that got broadly smarter — the two metrics have to be read together.

cards.heading: Structural hazard
cards.question: What is the structural hazard of training directly against the rubric's own evaluators?
cards.answer: It optimizes what the rubric measures — a proxy — rather than the actual goal the rubric stands in for.
